questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: New office safety technology after lockdown, and its problems
Why working from home is better than going to the office
How thermal cameras were first invented and used
How to design a modern, open-plan office space
questions.why: Sam says they'll look at how the new workplace technology works and ask if it's really the answer.

questions.q: Where is Sam during the programme?
options: Back in the BBC office
In a studio with Neil
Still working from home
Visiting a tech company
questions.why: Sam says, “still working from home, as you can hear.”

questions.q: Which technology might become 'the new normal' in workplaces?
options: Robots that clean and disinfect every desk at night
Plastic screens put up between every desk
Video calls instead of face-to-face meetings
Sensors, distance-alert apps and temperature devices
questions.why: Neil lists sensors that monitor movement, apps that alert you if you're too close, and temperature devices.

questions.q: How does Microshare's system work, according to Charles Paumelle?
options: Cameras film everyone who enters or leaves the building
Workers fill in a short health form every morning
Phones scan a special code at each door in the office
Bluetooth wristbands record when people are close
questions.why: He says staff wear Bluetooth wristbands or tags which detect proximity events.

questions.q: Why does the company save the proximity data?
options: To trace contacts if someone later becomes infected
To check how hard people are working at their desks
To sell it to other companies for a lot of money
To plan where desks should go in the new office
questions.why: Paumelle says it's saved in case they need to retrace an infected person's steps and inform contacts.

questions.q: What worry about this technology does Sam raise?
options: It is too expensive
It doesn't work with smartphones
It breaks easily
It feels like a big invasion of privacy
questions.why: Sam says it all feels like quite a big invasion of privacy.

questions.q: What does lawyer Ravi Naik suggest companies might be doing?
options: Breaking the law on purpose to save money
Spending too little on the safety of their staff
Using technology just for the sake of it
Ignoring what their workers want or need
questions.why: He asks, “are you trying to use tech for tech's sake?”

questions.q: What is Ravi Naik's opinion about the evidence for this technology?
options: There is plenty of evidence it works
There isn't enough evidence to justify it
Evidence isn't needed in a crisis
Only governments have the evidence
questions.why: He says there has to be a high level of evidential justification, and 'I just don't think it's there.'
